problem: The sentence reads "Z = 1 for an ideal gas, Z  1 when their size pushes them apart". The inequality sign is missing, so the sentence cannot be read, and the case Z < 1 (attraction dominating) is never stated. A student cannot tell which side of 1 means attraction and which means repulsion.
fix: The compressibility factor Z = PV/RT measures the departure from ideal behaviour: Z = 1 for an ideal gas, Z < 1 when attraction between molecules pulls them together, and Z > 1 when their own size pushes them apart (high pressure).

problem: The saturation temperature of water at exactly 1 bar (100 kPa) is 99.6 °C, not 99.97 °C. The value 99.97 °C belongs to about 1 atm. The step also calls 1 bar the "normal boiling pressure", but the normal boiling point is defined at 1 atm = 1.01325 bar, where water boils at 100.0 °C.
fix: At 1 bar the saturation temperature of water is 99.6 °C, close enough to call 100 °C for this example. The normal boiling point, 100 °C, is at 1 atm = 1.01325 bar, slightly above 1 bar. (The step-by-step conclusion, liquid at 25 °C, two-phase near 100 °C, vapour at 120 °C, does not change.)

problem: The symbol P is used for pressure throughout the chapter and then reused for the number of phases in F = C − P + 2 = 3 − P. A student skimming the formula can read it as "3 minus pressure".
fix: Keep the symbol but separate it clearly, for example F = C − P_ph + 2 = 3 − P_ph, where P_ph is the number of phases present and P alone always means pressure (in bar or Pa).

problem: The trap mixes the two diagrams. On a P–T diagram a point on the vaporisation curve is a two-phase state (saturated liquid and saturated vapour together), not "saturated liquid or saturated vapour". The wording "inside the dome two phases coexist" only applies to the P–V diagram.
fix: Reading the saturation curve as a single phase. On a P–T diagram every point of the vaporisation curve is a two-phase state: saturated liquid and saturated vapour together. On a P–V diagram the two branches of the dome are saturated liquid and saturated vapour, and only points strictly inside the dome are two-phase mixtures.

problem: "A rigid vessel" fixes the total volume, so within that vessel P and T cannot be varied independently. The answer then says both P and T are free (F = 2), which reads as a contradiction. The degrees of freedom are a property of the pure fluid, not of the container.
fix: Ask: "A sample of water is at 1 bar and 150 °C. How many degrees of freedom does it have, and what phase is it?" Answer as given: superheated vapour, one phase, F = 3 − 1 = 2, because for a single phase of a pure fluid T and P can be chosen independently.

problem: The pressure axis is linear from 0 to 250 bar, so the triple point (0.006 bar) and the whole low-pressure part of the vaporisation curve sit on the y-axis and are invisible. The figure does not show the steep shape of the curve or where the 1 bar line crosses it.
fix: Plot pressure on a logarithmic axis (or use an inset for 0–2 bar), so the triple point, the 1 bar crossing at about 100 °C and the critical point are all readable. Keep a note that pressure is on a log scale.
